channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Japan Credit Rating upgraded India from BBB+ to A-, its first change since 2007, as commerce minister Piyush Goyal said the US agreement will be finalised only once Washington offers tariff terms better than those of India's competitors.
item.description:
JCR cited fiscal consolidation, strong economic growth, resilient external finances and a healthier financial system, and raised the country ceiling by a notch to A; it had held India at BBB+ through the global financial crisis, the pandemic and subsequent geopolitical disruption. On trade, Goyal's condition is comparative rather than absolute — India wants a margin over competing exporters, not simply lower tariffs. Negotiations on the first phase have slowed because of shifting US trade policy, court rulings and new tariff measures and investigations; a senior US official said in July that the text was effectively finalised and could be signed within three to four months, with Section 301 investigations the main remaining hurdle. The agreement announced on 3 February reduces US tariffs on Indian goods, protects Indian agriculture and dairy, benefits textiles and smaller enterprises, and commits India to eliminating or reducing tariffs on all US industrial goods and a range of food and agricultural products, and to purchasing more than USD 500 billion of American energy, technology and other products. Goyal also listed further pacts expected with Israel, the Gulf Cooperation Council, the Southern African Customs Union, Mercosur, Chile, Mexico and Canada, and separately the India–New Zealand agreement signed in April is expected to take effect next month, under which New Zealand eliminates duties on all Indian goods and commits USD 20 billion of investment in India over fifteen years.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rating change and the trade stance point the same way: India is negotiating from a stronger position than a year ago and is willing to let a signed text wait. For manufacturers supplying Indian operations, the relevant detail is that the pending agreement would remove or cut Indian tariffs on all US industrial goods, which would change relative landed costs between US and European sources into India whenever it takes effect. The widening set of Indian trade agreements has a similar effect from other origins. Points that may be worth considering include how Indian import duties on industrial inputs are assumed in current sourcing plans, and whether the New Zealand agreement's expected entry into force next month affects any product flows.

LiveMint | The Economic Times | The Hindu Business Line | The Times of India | Business Standard

item.title: UPM is investing EUR 1.3 billion in its biorefinery at Leuna in Saxony-Anhalt, where the state parliament is elected on Sunday with the AfD polling far ahead and in reach of an absolute majority.
item.description:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned of the economic and social consequences of a possible AfD state government during his second campaign visit to the state, and separately visited the Leuna Chemical Park — described as the heart of Saxony-Anhalt's industry — in support of CDU minister-president Sven Schulze. The campaign itself is being run at a distance: reporting notes Merz has limited his appointments in the state to a minimum and is avoiding market-square appearances, and Green party leader Felix Banaszak said he is campaigning without voters. One exchange in the duel between Schulze and AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund turned on labour supply, with Siegmund arguing the state must meet its own demand for skilled workers through vocational orientation in schools and less bureaucracy, and Schulze rejecting that as too general and arguing the state needs immigration into the labour market. The reporting does not set out a timetable or scope for the UPM investment beyond the amount and the site.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A EUR 1.3 billion commitment to a bio-based production site is a signal about where European feedstock capacity is being built, and it is going to a location described as the heart of the state's industry. The political question sits on top rather than beside it: an AfD-led state government would put investment decisions of this size into an environment where planning approvals, energy policy and labour migration are all contested at state level, and the labour argument between the two lead candidates is precisely the one that determines whether a chemical park can staff an expansion. Points that may be worth considering include whether bio-based feedstock sourcing plans account for capacity coming on stream at Leuna, and how state-level political risk in eastern Germany is treated in site planning that assumes stable permitting.

Wallstreet:online | Handelsblatt | Yahoo Germany

item.title: Gulf aluminium producers, including Emirates Global Aluminium and Bahrain's Alba, face lower output, disrupted exports and stronger competition as the Iran war and a 50% US import levy reshape trade flows, with Brent near USD 95.
item.description:
The mechanism runs through the Strait of Hormuz in both directions. Iranian retaliation against Gulf states after the US and Israeli attacks that began on 28 February damaged local smelters and led to the effective closure of the strait, imperilling both the inbound flow of alumina, aluminium's feedstock, and the outbound movement of processed metal. The 50% US levy on most aluminium imports, in place since early last year, had already complicated sales as buyers met higher prices. The analysts quoted add a third element: stalled US–Canada trade talks mean Canadian producers, the world's fourth largest, may pivot to third markets if they lose American access, intensifying competition just as Gulf output is constrained. Oil itself eased slightly on the day, with November Brent at USD 94.98, down 0.7%, after three sessions of gains, as profit-taking met comments from Trump that eased concerns about the conflict's duration and as higher flows through Hormuz reduced perceived supply risk. The flow figures are disputed: TankerTrackers.com put 9.14 million barrels leaving the Arabian Sea on 31 August, while the US energy secretary claimed more than 17 million barrels moved through Hormuz by ship that day, a figure the tracker suggests may aggregate several days. German reporting notes Brent recently approached USD 100 and that gas wholesale prices rose sharply with the latest escalation.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Aluminium is where the energy shock becomes a materials shock, and the Gulf constraint arrives alongside a possible Canadian redirection rather than after it, so regional premia may move before any change in global supply totals. The alumina flow is the part that is easy to overlook: a smelter can be undamaged and still curtail output if feedstock cannot reach it. For packaging and automotive applications the practical exposure is through customers' metal costs and availability rather than through direct purchases. Points that may be worth considering include whether aluminium-intensive customer segments are modelled with regional rather than global price assumptions, and how the dispute over Hormuz flow data affects confidence in current energy cost forecasts.

CNAS | Anadolu Agency | Wirtschafts Woche | Fortune | The Nation

item.title: Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller said he is inclined to hold rates steady in September if data confirm inflation is cooling, cutting market odds of a rise to 50.4% from 63.2%, while the yen gained 1.4% to JPY 156.40.
item.description:
Waller left the alternative open, saying a rise at the 15–16 September meeting could be considered if inflation persists, and noting that the current 3.50%–3.75% policy rate is only slightly restrictive so it may not take much acceleration in inflation to move him toward tightening. Markets took the dovish reading: all three major US indexes closed at least 1% higher on 3 September, with the Nasdaq lifted by the large AI-related stocks, and CME's FedWatch odds for a September rise fell from 63.2% the previous day. The Fed's Beige Book described moderate growth since early July and a positive overall outlook, but reported household and business confidence under pressure from policy uncertainty, high energy prices and the Iran war, with consumers very sensitive to prices while demand for high-priced goods stayed strong. The currency move ran the other way from the rate move. The yen rose 1.4% to JPY 156.40 against the dollar, building on a 0.9% gain the day before and briefly strengthening by more than JPY 3 in New York trading, on expectations that the Bank of Japan will raise rates in mid-September; market participants generally judged that Tokyo had not intervened. Japan sold a tranche of 30-year bonds successfully, easing some of the pressure from the global bond selloff, though board member Hajime Takata has called for faster-paced rate rises and fiscal 2027 budget requests are expected to reach JPY 140 trillion against last year's record JPY 122.3 trillion.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The Federal Reserve is now expected to hold while the Bank of Japan is expected to raise in mid-September, and the currency has already started to price that divergence: the yen moved 1.4% in a single session. For European exporters the mechanical effect is on relative competitiveness against Japanese suppliers rather than on financing costs. The Beige Book's specific finding — consumers very sensitive to prices, but high-ticket demand holding — describes a market where price increases pass through unevenly by category rather than uniformly. Points that may be worth considering include how yen exposure is hedged into the mid-September Bank of Japan meeting, and whether US pricing plans distinguish between price-sensitive and high-ticket categories in the way the Beige Book describes.

The Economic Times | The Straits Times | The Financial Times | The Mainichi | Business Recorder | Commercial Times

item.title: A Canadian Federation of Independent Business survey found 18% of affected small exporters and 11% of small importers would stop being viable if the trade war lasts three months or more, days before Canada's 8 September counter-tariffs.
item.description:
The exposure is broad: 49% of small importers and 46% of small exporters have products directly hit by the latest round of tariffs and counter-tariffs, with manufacturing, wholesale, retail and construction the most affected sectors. Ottawa's countermeasures cover almost 900 US products from 8 September, including 25% on facial tissue and toilet paper, 50% on raw wood pulp, napkins and paper towels, 25% on US seafood and 50% on dairy other than cheese at 25%; Trump is threatening to double tariffs to 50% if no deal is reached by 1 January 2027. Deloitte Canada modelled the tail risk, putting the loss at 1.6% of real GDP, or $402 billion over the next decade, with employment 163,000 lower on average each year, if CUSMA is dismantled — a scenario the authors call a possibility that cannot be dismissed, given that the US took about 70% of Canadian exports in 2025. The political exchange hardened in parallel: Trump warned Carney against making him an enemy, saying such a stance could hurt Canada's economy, while Carney said Canada is ready to negotiate when Washington is, and announced CAD 4.7 billion to build and maintain VIA Rail passenger cars domestically for the first time in four decades. Ottawa also set out a CAD 7.5 billion support package, including CAD 1.5 billion through a Regional Tariff Response Initiative and a CAD 500 million liquidity stream under the Business Development Bank's Pivot to Grow programme, with the minimum revenue requirement lowered to CAD 1 million. One converter reports the effect directly: Eco Guardian's new Aurora plant in Ontario, with capacity above a billion paper cups a year, says enquiries from potential new customers surged over the past fortnight, while the Canada Border Services Agency opened subsidy and dumping investigations into paperboard containers and cups from China on 17 August, with preliminary determinations due on 16 November.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Paper and packaging is the category where the two Canadian measures compound. Pulp, tissue, napkins and towels from the US carry 25% to 50% from 8 September, while paperboard containers and cups from China face possible provisional duties from 16 November, which leaves domestic converting as the route with no new duty attached. The CFIB figures put a timetable rather than a magnitude on the risk in the customer base: 18% of affected small exporters describe three months as the limit, which is shorter than most contract review cycles. Points that may be worth considering include which Canadian converting customers fall inside the small-business definition the survey uses, and whether the November CBSA determination is being tracked alongside the September tariff date.

Financial Post | Fortune | BNN Bloomberg | The Times of India | The Economic Times | Financial Post | Financial Post | BNN Bloomberg

item.title: China's commerce ministry said trade talks with the EU cannot be driven by unilateral demands or threats of market closure, and Siemens chief executive Roland Busch said he opposes blanket EU tariffs on China.
item.description:
Spokeswoman Huang Ling made the remarks at a regular briefing on 3 September, framed as a response to EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's warnings about trade-defence instruments and market closure if negotiations fail to produce results. Huang said neither side should dictate terms or resort to threats of closing its market as a bargaining chip, and urged the EU to stand by free trade and the WTO-centred multilateral system. She also noted that the two sides have maintained close communication at various levels since the first meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism on 29 June, and said Beijing has been working to manage frictions and differences. The corporate counterpoint carried by Chinese state media pairs Busch's opposition to blanket tariffs with Slovak prime minister Robert Fico's comment to European Council president António Costa that Europe should not create barriers or treat China as an enemy, presenting both as evidence of a broader current in European industry and among pragmatic member states rather than as isolated remarks — a framing that comes from the outlet rather than from an independent assessment.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The negotiating positions on both sides are now public, which usually narrows the room for a quiet settlement and lengthens the timetable. For manufacturers with production in both blocs, the specific risk named is not tariffs alone but market closure used as leverage, which would reach export flows in either direction rather than only the goods under dispute. The presence of a large German industrial chief executive on the record against blanket measures indicates that at least some major European industrial firms are not aligned behind the Commission's harder options, which is itself a signal about how far those options can travel. Points that may be worth considering include which product flows would be caught by a defensive measure applied at sector rather than product level, and how Chinese production for European customers is currently treated in scenario planning.

China Daily | Global Times | Global Times | Xinhua

item.title: Plastics Europe says Europe's transition to circular plastics is losing momentum and wants the Circular Economy Act to accelerate circularity while supporting industry, as BCG puts over EUR 65 billion of unused raw materials in the EU's e-waste.
item.description:
Virginia Janssens, managing director of Plastics Europe, argues Europe has reached a critical moment and must act with more urgency, coordination and political commitment if it is to preserve industrial capacity while advancing circular objectives. The competitiveness problems she names are high energy and carbon costs, growing global overcapacity, rising imports and trade distortions — a list that places the association's case for the Act on industrial grounds alongside the environmental ones. The BCG study, produced with the Cradle to Cradle Electronics initiative, approaches the same question from the materials side: about 1.6 million tonnes of critical and strategic raw materials including copper, aluminium, lithium, cobalt and rare earths enter the EU market inside new devices each year, and most come from third countries, primarily China, which the authors describe as holding a near-monopoly in heavy rare earths. Their conclusion is that product design has to change fundamentally toward circular principles. Plastics Europe Deutschland is holding an innovation press conference at the Haus der Bundespressekonferenz on 11 September at which BASF, Covestro, Dow, Evonik, LyondellBasell, Röhm and others are due to present circular economy and climate-neutral production solutions.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Both documents point at product design rather than at waste handling, and design-for-disassembly is where adhesive technologies enter the argument directly: a bonded joint that cannot be separated economically keeps the materials inside it out of recovery. If the Circular Economy Act translates the competitiveness framing into design requirements, debonding performance becomes a compliance property alongside bond strength rather than a customer preference. The BCG figure also frames recovered materials as a supply-security question rather than only an environmental one, which tends to attract different budget holders. Points that may be worth considering include how debonding-on-demand capability is positioned in electronics and appliance applications, and whether the 11 September press conference is a useful read on where large European producers expect the Act to land.

Plastics Europe | Wirtschafts Woche | Plastics Europe Deutschland

item.title: The crisis in parts of Germany's paper, board and packaging industry is worsening under high energy and CO₂ costs and difficult markets, with recent insolvencies and the closure of Baiersbronn Frischfaser Karton after its investor withdrew.
item.description:
The recycling association BVSE describes the closure as an illustration of how tense the situation has become rather than as an isolated case. There had been hope of continuing Baiersbronn Frischfaser Karton through an investor process; according to media reports the potential investor withdrew at the end of August, which the association says means continuation beyond the opening of insolvency proceedings is no longer possible. The pressures named are high energy and CO₂ costs together with difficult market conditions, the first two of which are structural rather than cyclical. No figures are given for capacity lost or for the number of affected plants, and the source is a sector association rather than an official statistics body, so the reading available is a qualitative one: capacity in German board production is being removed through insolvency rather than through planned restructuring.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Board and carton capacity leaving the German market through insolvency has a different profile from planned closures, because it removes supply without a transition period and concentrates remaining volume on fewer converters. For anyone selling into carton and corrugated converting, the near-term question is continuity of specific customers rather than sector demand, and the medium-term one is whether European board supply tightens enough to move prices. The energy and CO₂ cost drivers also apply upstream of converting, which means the pressure is unlikely to be confined to fibre producers. Points that may be worth considering include which German carton and board customers appear in current receivables and volume plans, and whether alternative converting capacity has been identified for the affected regions.

BVSE

item.title: The paints and coatings industry in German-speaking Europe is entering a new consolidation era, with BASF's coatings sale to Carlyle and QIA, the planned Akzo Nobel–Axalta merger and Henkel's purchase of Stahl named as the shaping deals.
item.description:
The trade reporting describes a fundamental transformation of the sector's mergers and acquisitions market across 2025 and 2026, characterised by billion-euro transactions, strategic repositioning and renewed investor appetite. The pressure is described as falling unevenly: large players are pursuing transformational mergers and financial investors are re-entering, while small and medium-sized companies face mounting pressure to reach scale or consolidate. The article does not give deal values, completion dates or market-share figures, so the claim to weigh is directional — that ownership in this part of the specialty chemicals chain is changing hands at an accelerating rate, and that private equity and sovereign capital are now among the buyers alongside strategic acquirers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Consolidation among coatings makers changes the counterparty landscape on both sides of a formulator's business at once, since the same companies are often customers, competitors in adjacent applications and buyers of similar raw materials. Where financial investors take ownership of a division carved out of a larger group, purchasing behaviour and specification stability can change on a different timetable than under strategic ownership. The pressure described on smaller firms is the part with the clearest second-order effect, because pressure to reach scale tends to consolidate a supplier base faster than any single transaction does. Points that may be worth considering include how a smaller supplier base in this segment would affect negotiating positions on shared raw materials, and whether adjacency planning treats coatings consolidation as a competitive or a customer development.

European Coatings

item.title: German chemical and pharmaceutical sales rose 7.3% in the second quarter, their first increase in three years, driven mainly by a 5.7% price rise the VCI attributes to war-related supply problems for Asian and Middle Eastern rivals.
item.description:
The composition of the increase is the point. The VCI attributes it to production rising 2.4% on the previous quarter and prices 5.7%. The VCI's explanation is that competitors in Asia and the Middle East are more dependent than European producers on transport through the Strait of Hormuz, and that many customers have replenished stocks in view of the Iran war — which makes the gain a function of a disrupted trade route and of restocking rather than of recovered underlying demand. Against that, Henning Block, a partner at Rothschild & Co, said he is currently a bit more worried about the German chemical industry than about the automotive industry, noting that 5% more companies filed for insolvency in the first five months of 2026 than in the same period of 2025, and that the situation is unlikely to normalise until framework conditions support more sustainable growth. The VCI has separately argued that Germany should become the world's leading centre for chemistry, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, while warning that laws such as the health insurance reform are slowing industrial value creation, and that if rhetoric and action keep diverging the country becomes a sales market for international competitors rather than a production location.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A sales recovery built mainly on price, with volumes moving 2.4%, reads differently from one built on demand, and the association itself ties the price component to a shipping route and to customer restocking. Both are reversible: if Hormuz traffic normalises or stocks are worked down, the price support weakens without any change in European competitiveness. The insolvency figure Block cites is for companies generally rather than for chemicals alone, and it sits alongside the sales gain rather than contradicting it, since headline sector revenue and the survival of individual suppliers can move in opposite directions. Points that may be worth considering include how much of the current European price level is assumed to persist in 2027 planning, and whether supplier risk monitoring reflects a rising insolvency rate among German companies.

Wallstreet:online | Wirtschafts Woche | Politico Europe

item.title: Volkswagen's board approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade, the largest restructuring in the global car industry, with unions and management agreeing the future of four German plants cannot be guaranteed.
item.description:
No closures have been approved. The four sites named are Neckarsulm, Zwickau, Emden and Hannover, and alternative uses are being considered. The company is facing US tariffs, weak electric-vehicle demand and intensifying Chinese competition, and said aligning workforce levels with economic realities is essential. Reporting on the labour question puts German automotive labour costs at around USD 3,307 per vehicle, against USD 597 in China and USD 955 in Spain, with the 35-hour week negotiated by IG Metall in the 1980s and 1990s still the full-time standard in metalworking. In the political response, SPD leader Bärbel Bas said state support for the industry must be tied to site guarantees, telling the Funke newspapers that companies cannot expect the state to create good framework conditions and then relocate production. Public opinion is with intervention — an Infratest dimap survey found 62% in favour of special government support against 32% against, with 81% calling the industry important or very important for Germany's economic future. The underlying production data remains weak while the demand mix shifts sharply: the VDA reported 229,900 cars built in Germany in August, down 4% year on year and 16% below 2019 for the year to date, with August exports down 12% and total orders down 11%, while the KBA recorded registrations up 2.6% and battery-electric registrations up 75% to a 32.4% share, private buyers up almost 17% and commercial registrations down more than 5%.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A cut of this size announced without plant closures points to attrition and shift reduction over several years rather than a step change in installed capacity, so the volume effect on suppliers is likely to be gradual and concentrated in the four named sites. The demand data underneath complicates the picture in a way that matters for materials: German output is falling while battery-electric registrations rise 75%, so the same market is shifting toward vehicles with different joining, sealing and thermal requirements even as the total shrinks. The commercial-fleet decline against a 17% private increase is a further mix change. Points that may be worth considering include how site-level exposure at Neckarsulm, Zwickau, Emden and Hannover is distributed across supply agreements, and whether product planning tracks the electric share of German registrations separately from total build volumes.

The Economic Times | Wirtschafts Woche | Wallstreet:online | The Economic Times | VDA | Handelsblatt

item.title: US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick says a semiconductor tariff is being prepared, and favours exempting foreign firms only if they invest in US chip manufacturing, as tariffs of up to 100% on imported drones took effect on 3 September.
item.description:
The chip measure is described as still in preparation, with a phased introduction under consideration. What is unusual is its potential reach: the duties could affect not only microchips but products in which they are installed, with games consoles, laptops and servers for data centres named, which would make the tariff base far wider than the semiconductor trade itself. Taiwanese reporting reads the design as aimed at Samsung and SK Hynix, on the argument that South Korea has been slow to deliver on US investment commitments; the two companies announced a combined KRW 800 trillion, close to USD 590 billion, for four memory fabs at home in late June. Separately, South Korea's industry ministry said four US firms will invest USD 2 billion there across energy, advanced materials and semiconductors, including Corning in glass and materials for chips and displays, Axcelis in ion implantation equipment and Air Products in rare and semiconductor gases at Pyeongtaek. The drone tariffs, signed on 13 August, took effect on 3 September: an additional 100% on drones above 25 kilograms take-off weight and on models with thermal imagers, docking stations and certain critical components, 25% on smaller drones, and a further 25% on other components from 9 February 2027. Qualifying products from the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland and Liechtenstein face a total ceiling of 15%, and British products 10%.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The design principle in both measures is the same, and it is the part that reaches suppliers: tariff relief is being tied to where a company invests rather than to what a product is. A levy that follows chips into finished goods would put duty on the assembled article, which changes the landed cost of equipment bought for plants rather than of any input, and the allied ceilings mean the same drone can carry 100%, 25%, 15% or 10% depending on origin. The February 2027 date on components gives a defined window before the second tranche. Points that may be worth considering include whether capital equipment orders with chip content are priced against the current tariff schedule, and how origin ceilings are being tracked for equipment sourced from allied suppliers.

Handelsblatt | Commercial Times | Hürriyet Daily News | The Economic Times | Channel News Asia
